## My Reasoning

I have worked this land in Quzhou for 40 years. I know the seasons, the soil, and what works. My 16.1 mu splits naturally — about 10 mu stays in my wheat-maize rotation, and the remaining 6.1 mu I keep in cotton. Cotton prices have been acceptable and the soil in that section responds well to it.

For wheat, I plant in early October after deep rotary tillage. I switched to improved varieties years ago — the yield gain is real and I have seen it over decades. I irrigate at overwintering, jointing, and grain fill — three times is usually enough with my well. I apply nitrogen in split doses: heavier at base, lighter at jointing. I watch for powdery mildew and aphids; two pesticide passes are standard for me.

For maize, I go straight into no-till after wheat harvest in June. No point disturbing the soil twice in a season. I use hybrid seed — Zhengdan or similar — and I know the nitrogen demand is front-loaded. Three irrigations carry me through a dry summer. Corn borer and fall armyworm have been problems in recent years, so I budget two pesticide applications.

Cotton gets the most labor and inputs from me. It needs deep ploughing in spring, more irrigations, and careful pest scouting all season. Bollworm management takes four to five pesticide passes in a bad year. I know this intimately. The potassium demand on cotton is higher than the grains, so I don't skimp there.

Being 62 with just two of us in the household, I am not expanding. I maintain what I know well.
